meta.audience: Ammon's brethren, the sons of Mosiah
meta.location: Among the Lamanites, at the end of the mission
meta.unit: The sons of Mosiah among the Lamanites (Alma 17–26)
principles: Joy that keeps its accounting straight

world_behind.title: This is the end of a fourteen-year mission
world_behind.text: Alma 17 began with the brothers separating; here they are together, counting what happened. The speech is a report delivered to the men who did the work.

world_behind.title: Ammon is quoting Alma's conversion
world_behind.text: Verse 3 has the Lamanites in the darkest abyss brought to behold the marvelous light of God. Mosiah 27 has Alma using the same two phrases of himself, and Ammon was in the room.

world_behind.title: Aaron interrupts
world_behind.text: Verse 10 has him rebuke his own brother mid-speech for boasting. The record keeps the objection and then gives Ammon twenty-five verses of answer.

world_behind.title: Their errand had been laughed at
world_behind.text: Verses 23 and 24 recall the Nephites in Zarahemla mocking the plan and listing the Lamanites' crimes as proof it would fail. Verse 25 says some proposed extermination instead.

world_behind.title: They nearly quit
world_behind.text: Verse 27 says their hearts were depressed and they were about to turn back. The comfort that came was a promise of success attached to a command to bear afflictions patiently.

world_behind.title: The abuse is itemized
world_behind.text: Verse 29 lists being cast out, mocked, spit upon, struck on the cheeks, stoned, bound with cords, and jailed. Alma 23 had banned the same list by decree, item for item.

world_behind.title: Ammon ranks the converts above his own nation
world_behind.text: Verses 33 and 34 put them above the Nephites, who would fight rather than be killed.

words.text: A curved blade for reaping grain. The word appears once in this record and twelve times in the King James Bible, most of them in harvest judgments. Ammon's line about thrusting in the sickle into a ripe field is nearly the wording of the angel in Revelation 14:15.

Wishes, pleases, chooses. An archaic form used five times in this record and twice in the King James Bible, where the wind blows where it listeth. Ammon uses it of the enemy's winds, which cannot carry away the people gathered into God's garners.

Without equal. It appears eight times in the record, and the King James Bible never. Four of the eight are king Benjamin and his son on the matchless power of God; Ammon attaches it instead to bounty, and to love.

One who repents. It appears seven times in this record and never in the King James Bible. Ammon makes it the entire qualification for knowing the things he has been describing, and verse 22 spells out what a penitent person actually does.
Being deprived of what one needs. The word occurs once in scripture. Ammon uses it to sum up fourteen years in one noun, then immediately lists the specifics in the next verse.

The inward parts, and in scripture the seat of compassion. The record uses it eight times and the King James Bible thirty-nine, always in this sense of felt mercy. Ammon ends the chapter with God's bowels of mercy over all the earth.

phrases.term: Behold the number of your sheaves
phrases.text: Ammon tells his brethren to look at the count. He has just described the field as ripe and the labor as all day long, and now he directs their attention to the result, which is a number of people.

phrases.term: I fear that thy joy doth carry thee away unto boasting
phrases.text: Aaron's whole contribution to the chapter, and it is a correction of his brother in front of the company. The record preserves the rebuke and lets Ammon answer it at length.

phrases.term: I know that I am nothing
phrases.text: The center of the answer. Ammon concedes his own weakness in five words and then says he will boast of God, who gives him strength for everything. Verse 36 comes back and accepts the word boasting on those terms.
Alma 5 had asked the people of Zarahemla whether they could still sing that song. Here Ammon reports thousands of Lamanites doing it, loosed from the pains of hell.

phrases.term: I cannot say the smallest part which I feel
phrases.text: Ammon stops in the middle of the praise to say the praise is inadequate. He has just asked who can glory too much in the Lord, and he answers his own rhetoric by admitting the language will not stretch.

phrases.term: There is none that knoweth these things, save it be the penitent
phrases.text: How knowing works, in this chapter, stated flatly. Knowledge of these things is restricted, and the gate is repentance. Verse 22 lists the requirements: repentance, faith, good works, and prayer without ceasing.
What their own people did when they announced the mission. Ammon recalls it exactly, including the argument that the Lamanites were too stiffnecked and too bloody to reach.

phrases.term: Bear with patience thine afflictions, and I will give unto you success
phrases.text: The comfort given at the point of turning back. The promise of success arrives bound to a requirement of patience under affliction, and the next verses show which came first.

phrases.term: We have traveled from house to house, relying upon the mercies of the world
phrases.text: Ammon corrects himself in the same breath, adding that it was the mercies of God they leaned on. The self-correction is left in the record, the way Mormon's is in Alma 24.

phrases.term: Has there been so great love in all the land? ... not, even among the Nephites
phrases.text: Ammon puts converted Lamanites above his own nation on the one measure he thinks counts. Verse 34 gives his reason: the Nephites would take up arms and refuse to be slain.

Ammon's name for his own people, a branch lost from the tree of Israel. He has spent the chapter on Lamanites and ends by putting Nephites in the same category, and then extends God's mindfulness to every people in every land.

verses.label: v. 1
verses.title: The abridger hands over the page
verses.text: The chapter opens on a formula: "these are the words of Ammon to his brethren, which say thus." Only two verses in the whole volume use that formula. The other is 1 Ne. 8:34, "These are the words of my father." Both mark the same act, a writer stopping his own account to let a document stand on its own, and in both cases what follows is speech he did not compose. Thirty-seven verses run from here to the chapter's end without one sentence of narration. Mormon does not reappear until the next chapter.

verses.label: v. 2–3
verses.title: A speaker who answers himself
verses.text: Verse 2 asks two questions and then asks whether anyone can answer them: "what great blessings has he bestowed upon us? Can ye tell?" Verse 3 replies "Behold, I answer for you." The chapter carries fifteen question marks across twelve of its thirty-seven verses, which is the third heaviest concentration in the book of Alma, behind Alma 5 with forty-two and Alma 30 with twenty-two. Both of those are cross-examinations with a hostile party present. This one has no opponent in the room, so every question is asked and answered by the same mouth.

verses.label: v. 10–12
verses.title: The record keeps the objection
verses.text: In the middle of the speech a listener interrupts, and the interruption is preserved in his own words: "his brother Aaron rebuked him, saying: Ammon, I fear that thy joy doth carry thee away unto boasting." Nothing requires this to be here. The chapter is Ammon's, the charge is against Ammon, and it is his brother making it. What follows is the answer, "I do not boast in my own strength, nor in my own wisdom," and then the concession that makes the answer honest: "I know that I am nothing; as to my strength I am weak."

verses.label: v. 24
verses.title: The mockery quoted, not summarised
verses.text: The chapter could have said that people in Zarahemla doubted the mission. Instead it gives their sentences: "Do ye suppose that ye can bring the Lamanites to the knowledge of the truth? Do ye suppose that ye can convince the Lamanites of the incorrectness of the traditions of their fathers?" Verse 23 introduces the exchange and verse 24 hands it over, with the marker "this was their language." It is the only place in the volume where the objection to this mission is preserved as speech, and the speaker who preserved it is the man it was aimed at.

verses.label: v. 31–34
verses.title: A phrase that exists only here
verses.text: Ammon accounts for the converts three times in four verses and uses the same explanation each time: "because of their love towards their brethren" (v. 31), "because of their love towards their brethren" (v. 32), and the argument repeats behind verse 34. The phrase because of their love occurs three times in the whole volume and all three are in this chapter, inside a span of four verses. A chapter about a mission ends up giving its result not as conversions counted but as a single motive named three times.

verses.label: v. 35–36
verses.title: The charge accepted on new terms
verses.text: The record has kept Aaron's word from verse 10, that joy "doth carry thee away unto boasting." Twenty-five verses later Ammon uses the same construction about himself: "my joy is carried away, even unto boasting in my God." Then verse 36 stops arguing: "Now if this is boasting, even so will I boast." The verb boast stands seven times in this chapter, more than twice as often as in any other chapter of the volume, with Mosiah 2 next at three. The speech denies the charge in verse 11 and grants it in verse 36, and the difference between the two is one prepositional phrase.

verses.label: v. 37
verses.title: The last claim is the widest
verses.text: After thirty-six verses about one mission to one people, the closing sentence drops the particulars: "God is mindful of every people, whatsoever land they may be in; yea, he numbereth his people, and his bowels of mercy are over all the earth." The phrase every people whatsoever land appears nowhere else in the volume. The chapter also uses rejoice seven times, which is more than any other chapter in the volume or in the Bible, and it spends the last of them not on the converts but on a claim about everyone the speaker has never met.

chapter.title: The rebuke stays in the record
chapter.text: The rebuke is quoted at verse 10, "Ammon, I fear that thy joy doth carry thee away unto boasting," and the answer runs from verse 11 to verse 12 in two parts, a denial, "I do not boast in my own strength, nor in my own wisdom," and a concession, "I know that I am nothing; as to my strength I am weak." Verse 36 returns to the charge and accepts it on new terms, "Now if this is boasting, even so will I boast." A rejoicing chapter keeps the objection to its own rejoicing and answers it twice.

chapter.title: Ammon redefines the word instead of denying the charge
chapter.text: He grants that he is nothing and claims all the strength as God's, then in verse 36 says that if this is boasting he will boast. The argument is settled by relocating the subject.

chapter.title: He quotes Alma's conversion at people who were there
chapter.text: Darkest abyss and marvelous light are Alma's words about himself in Mosiah 27. Ammon applies them to a nation and says nothing about the borrowing.

chapter.title: Knowledge is tied to repentance
chapter.text: Verse 21 puts the mysteries out of reach of the natural man and inside the reach of the penitent, and verse 22 makes the qualification a set of practices instead of a status.

chapter.title: The mission almost ended before it began
chapter.text: Verse 27 has them depressed and turning back. Fourteen years of results rest on a moment that could have gone the other way, and Ammon reports it in the middle of the celebration.

chapter.title: The cost is listed beside the harvest
chapter.text: Stoning, spitting, cords, and prison sit in the same speech as the sheaves and the garners. The chapter refuses to give the joy without the ledger.

chapter.title: He ranks his own nation second
chapter.text: No people match them here, the Nephites included, because Nephites fight back. It is a hard thing for a Nephite prince to say to Nephites.

chapter.title: The last verse is about everyone else
chapter.text: The last verse widens the frame in three clauses: "God is mindful of every people, whatsoever land they may be in," "he numbereth his people," and "his bowels of mercy are over all the earth." Nothing in the preceding thirty-six verses concerns anyone outside one mission to one nation. Verse 23 has recorded what the Zarahemla Nephites thought of that mission, "they laughed us to scorn," so a chapter that begins with a people written off ends with a claim that no people is.

applications.title: Count the sheaves out loud
applications.text: Ammon told his co-workers to look at the harvest, "behold the number of your sheaves!" People who have worked hard are usually the last to have counted, and somebody has to say the number.

applications.title: Answer the correction instead of dismissing it
applications.text: Aaron said the joy was carrying him into boasting, and Ammon neither ignored it nor collapsed under it. He denied one thing, "I do not boast in my own strength," and conceded another, "I know that I am nothing." Both halves in two verses.

applications.title: Say what you can do and who it belongs to
applications.text: The full sentence is "as to my strength I am weak... for in his strength I can do all things." Neither half stands alone in the chapter. A statement of capacity with its source attached is more useful than either modesty or confidence by itself.

applications.title: Say who you did not come to destroy
applications.text: The purpose is stated in the negative first, "we came into the wilderness not with the intent to destroy our brethren, but with the intent that perhaps we might save some few of their souls." Naming what you are not doing is part of describing what you are.

applications.title: Keep going when the promise comes with a condition
applications.text: At the point of turning back the comfort arrives with work attached, "bear with patience thine afflictions, and I will give unto you success." The encouragement does not remove the affliction; it puts an outcome on the far side of it.

applications.title: List the places you actually went
applications.text: Houses, streets, hills, temples, synagogues. The record itemizes the venues rather than summarizing the effort. When you take stock of something you have done, name the specific occasions; the list is the honest form of the claim.

applications.title: Set the bar at "some few" and then look up
applications.text: They supposed their joy would be full if they could save one soul, and verse 31 asks the question afterward, "are they few? I say unto you, Nay, they are many." Aim at the number you could bear to get, and count what actually came.

applications.title: Widen the claim at the end
applications.text: After thirty-six verses about one mission, the closing sentence drops the particulars, "God is mindful of every people, whatsoever land they may be in; yea, he numbereth his people." A specific success is a poor place to stop, and this one opens onto everybody.

questions.text: What have I labored at long enough to be able to count the result?
When someone last told me my enthusiasm had gone somewhere wrong, what did I do with it?
What would it change if I said out loud that I am nothing and meant it as a fact rather than as self-criticism?
What do I feel about God that I cannot say the smallest part of?
Which of the four things in verse 22 am I currently not doing?
What am I on the edge of turning back from?
Whose love have I been slow to admit exceeds my own people's?
